study_identification_part.si4_title: Delineating the Heterogeneity of Alzheimer’s Disease and Mild Cognitive Impairment Using Normative Models of Dynamic Brain Functional Networks

cm1_research_objectives.reason: The abstract and introduction clearly state the research questions and purpose of using normative modeling: to quantify individual-level deviations in dynamic functional connectivity (dFC) and use these deviation patterns to identify and compare AD and MCI subtypes, including brain/clinical differences and longitudinal trajectories. This satisfies both criteria (objectives stated; purpose of normative modeling described).
cm1_research_objectives.supporting_text:
METHODS: We constructed sex-specific normative age models of dynamic brain functional networks and mapped the deviations ... Then, based on these individual deviation patterns, subtypes for both AD and MCI were identified using the clustering method, and their similarities and differences were comprehensively assessed.
In the current study, we aimed to elucidate the heterogeneity of MCI and identify robust subtypes of AD and MCI based on dynamic functional characteristics. ... we mapped individuals' features from heterogeneous cohorts to a normative model and generated interpretable deviation features to identify potential subtypes ... The neurophysiological traits of different subtypes were analyzed based on brain morphology and cognitive scores.

nm1_selection_criteria_reference_cohort.reason: This study builds a new normative model using Dataset 1 (Cam-CAN). They cite the open dataset and specify it comprises healthy individuals (eligibility via source citation), and they report the final sample size (n=644). They mention conducting quality control, but do not detail explicit image quality thresholds or exclusion reasons for Dataset 1 in the main text; details are deferred to prior work/supplement. Thus: eligibility/source cited (Yes); image quality standards (unclear for Dataset 1); final sample size reported (Yes).
nm1_selection_criteria_reference_cohort.supporting_text:
Dataset 1, which included 644 healthy individuals, was used in this work to build a normative model and was obtained from the Cambridge Centre for Aging and Neuroscience repository (Cam-CAN ...).
All the fMRI scans from 3 datasets were preprocessed ... After quality control, we obtained a regional fMRI signal ... Detailed information is provided in our previous study ... and can be found in the Supplemental Method S2.

nm2_handling_of_covariates_reference_coh.reason: The normative models explicitly include age and sex as covariates when training on the healthy reference cohort (Dataset 1). Dataset 1 is single-site, so site-effects handling is not applicable for model building.
nm2_handling_of_covariates_reference_coh.supporting_text: We estimated normative models to predict each dFC feature using sex and age as covariates in Gaussian process regression ... in a large healthy reference cohort from dataset 1.

nm6_internal_data_validation_reference_c.reason: They used 10-fold cross-validation on Dataset 1 to assess generalizability prior to training the final model on the full reference cohort.
nm6_internal_data_validation_reference_c.supporting_text: To assess the generalizability of the model, we used 10-fold cross-validation before applying the model trained on datasets 1 to dataset 2 and dataset 3.

nm7_external_data_validation_reference_c.reason: They applied the normative model trained on Dataset 1 to independent external datasets (Dataset 2 and Dataset 3) that include healthy controls and patients. However, they do not report a dedicated external validation focused solely on healthy individuals' fit/calibration; the external application is primarily for deviation mapping and downstream analyses.
nm7_external_data_validation_reference_c.supporting_text: ... before applying the model trained on datasets 1 to dataset 2 and dataset 3.

nm8_normative_modeling_approach.reason: They specify the modeling approach (Gaussian process regression) and covariates (age, sex) and that 34 models were fit for dFC features, with 10-fold CV. However, key settings (e.g., kernel type, priors) and implementation libraries are not detailed in the main text; software packages for normative modeling are not explicitly named.
nm8_normative_modeling_approach.supporting_text: We estimated normative models to predict each dFC feature using sex and age as covariates in Gaussian process regression ... In this study, 34 normative models could be built to predict each feature of the dFC pattern (17 a-FCS and 17 f-FCS features, respectively).

The distribution and brain map of the standardized mean squared error (SMSE) (A) and the mean squared log-loss (MSLL) (B) between observed and predicted overall functional connectivity strengths in the Dataset 1 under 10-fold cross-validation.

cr6_interpretation_of_deviation_scores.reason: They interpret the direction and meaning of deviation scores (positive vs negative deviations indicating increased vs decreased dFC in specific networks) and discuss clinical implications (subtype differences, potential progression). However, they do not define explicit quantitative thresholds (e.g., |Z|>1.96) for categorizing extremes.
cr6_interpretation_of_deviation_scores.supporting_text: We identified subtypes with positive deviation patterns ... and the others with negative deviations. Positive deviation patterns for AD and MCI were both mainly in the SM and DAN, indicating increased dFC strength and fluctuations. The functional connectivity strength in the DMN of AD-2 and MCI-2 decreased significantly. ... These results highlight that decreased dynamic functional patterns were associated with a high risk of conversion from MCI to AD.
